claims.text: A machine-learning framework can integrate ab initio-derived information for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Descriptors of local atomic configurations and short-range order can be used to predict phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
Such descriptors improve predictions by better quantifying disorder-induced phonon scattering.
The proposed model will reduce predictive error by approximately 20% relative to traditional methods.
Configurational disorder is the dominant influence on phonon scattering and thermal transport in the targeted multicomponent disordered HEAs, including BCC systems.
The model is trained on ab initio descriptors of local bonding environments, lattice mismatch, and phonon dispersion.
The approach is applicable from room temperature to approximately 900 °C.
The approach is applicable only where disorder-induced scattering governs thermal conductivity.
Descriptors of local configuration and short-range order reflect distributions of bonding environments and lattice distortions.
The descriptor representation mediates the relationship between alloy composition and enhanced phonon scattering.
Ab initio descriptors encode the effects of local disorder on phonon-scattering rates.
Correlating these descriptors with measured thermal properties will improve prediction of low thermal conductivity.
Empirical correlations, effective-medium theories, and standard molecular-dynamics simulations average disorder effects and fail to capture local variability in phonon scattering.
The model's accuracy will deteriorate for alloys with pronounced phase separation, long-range ordering, or compositions far outside its training set.
Alloys classified as low-conductivity by the model will exhibit approximately 20% lower predictive error than predictions from empirical or mean-field methods.
TDTR or laser-flash analysis can provide the thermal-conductivity measurements needed to benchmark the model over the proposed temperature range.
A predicted low-conductivity alloy exceeding its predicted range by more than a 20% error margin would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The main performance claim is an approximately 20% reduction in predictive error relative to competing methods, whereas the falsification rule treats 20% as an absolute error margin for an individual prediction. These are different quantities, so the stated rule does not directly test the claimed comparative improvement.
